implementation_notes: Sequence is Kotlin's pull-based lazy pipeline: asSequence() turns a collection or Iterable into a chain whose intermediate operators (filter, map, flatMap, windowed, chunked) return new sequences and are evaluated only by a terminal operation such as toList, first or forEach, so no intermediate lists are built and the sequence's iterator is the pipe. It replaces the classic Filter/Pipe structure entirely for in-process transformations. Use Flow when the source is asynchronous, hot, or when stages must run on different dispatchers.
code_sketch:
val report = orders.asSequence()          // lazy source
    .filter { it.total > 0 }              // stage 1
    .map { it.withTax(taxRate) }          // stage 2
    .sortedBy { it.date }
    .toList()                             // terminal op drives the chain
pitfalls: Mixing lazy Sequence operators with eager List operators re-materialises the collection per stage and destroys the laziness the pipeline was built for.
A sequence cannot be iterated twice; a second terminal operation re-runs the whole chain including side effects.
Sequence pipelines are single-threaded by construction: a blocking stage blocks the caller, unlike Flow which can move work with flowOn.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Flow stages
variants.idiom_name: Flow<T> with filter/map/flowOn, collected with suspend collect{}
variants.implementation_notes: Flow is the asynchronous counterpart with the same operator names: a cold stream emits from a suspending builder (flow {} / flowOf / callbackFlow) and stages are composed with filter, map, transform, buffer and conflate, executed on the dispatcher chosen by flowOn, while a slow collector suspends the producer and thereby applies backpressure. Choose Flow over Sequence when a stage performs I/O, when stages must run concurrently, or when cancellation and timeouts must propagate through the chain; the coroutine machinery is unnecessary overhead for pure in-memory transformations.
variants.code_sketch:
fun stage(src: Flow<String>): Flow<Record> = src
    .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
    .map { Record.parse(it) }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)         // upstream runs off the collector's context

file.readLines().asFlow()
    .let(::stage)
    .collect { sink.write(it) }          // collector pace throttles the producer
pitfalls: An unbounded buffer() between stages removes backpressure and turns a slow collector into memory growth; only buffer with a size you can justify.
flowOn changes the context of upstream operators only - blocking calls placed after it still block the collector's dispatcher.
Flow builders are cold and per-collector: collecting twice repeats the source (which matters for side-effecting stages); use shareIn/stateIn for hot data.
